triage.name: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
triage.reason: Premature infant with grunting, retractions and cyanosis; diagnosis reachable from history, exam, blood gas and chest x-ray, with important look-alikes such as sepsis and transient tachypnea.

age.peak: 0 (newborn; risk falls as gestational age rises, greatest below 28 weeks)

demographics: Risk is inversely related to gestational age and birth weight; it is uncommon at term
More common in infants of diabetic mothers and in those delivered by cesarean section without labor
Male infants are affected somewhat more often than female infants
Occurs in all racial and ethnic groups

risk_factors.text: Low birth weight for gestational age
Family history of respiratory distress syndrome in a sibling

family_history: Respiratory distress syndrome in a previous sibling

chief_complaints.text: He's breathing fast and making a grunting noise
His chest is pulling in when he breathes
He looks blue around the lips
He was born early and is having trouble breathing

hpi.onset: Within minutes to the first few hours after birth; symptoms are present by 6 hours of age in nearly all affected infants
hpi.duration: Progressive over the first 24–72 hours, then gradually improves with treatment
hpi.progression: Starts as rapid breathing and nasal flaring shortly after delivery, then worsens over the first day with grunting, retractions and worsening cyanosis; peaks around 48–72 hours and slowly resolves over days to weeks depending on gestational age
hpi.quality: Labored breathing with audible grunting on expiration and visible pulling in of the chest wall
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; often requires supplemental oxygen and respiratory support
hpi.timing: Continuous and worsening over the first 2–3 days of life

associated_symptoms.text: Pulling in of the chest wall between and below the ribs
Bluish color of the lips and skin
Low oxygen level on the monitor

pertinent_negatives: Fever or temperature instability suggesting infection
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid or meconium aspiration at delivery
Prolonged rupture of membranes or maternal chorioamnionitis
Cough or runny nose in the mother or household contacts
Congenital heart murmur or known cardiac defect

positives.text: Bluish discoloration of lips and skin

negatives: Difference in blood pressure between arms and legs
argues_against: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

atypical.how_it_differs: Late preterm and near-term infants may have milder or delayed symptoms, sometimes presenting after 6 hours of age with only tachypnea and mild retractions.
Infants of diabetic mothers may develop respiratory distress despite being near term or term, and may have macrosomia and hypoglycemia.

general.mild: Alert, pink, breathing comfortably fast with mild nasal flaring; tolerates handling
general.moderate: Tachypneic with audible grunting and visible retractions; startles and desaturates with handling
general.severe: Ill-appearing, dusky, marked grunting and retractions, poor tone; desaturates without support
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, cyanotic, apneic or gasping, flaccid, unresponsive to stimulation

findings.maneuver: Count the respiratory rate over a full minute while the infant is calm
Listen at the mouth and nose with the infant undisturbed
findings.finding: Audible expiratory grunting with each breath

findings.maneuver: Observe the nares during quiet breathing
findings.finding: Flaring of the alae nasi with inspiration

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest wall during inspiration
findings.finding: Inward pulling of the intercostal spaces

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lower chest and upper abdomen during inspiration
findings.finding: Inward pulling below the costal margin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the suprasternal notch during inspiration
findings.finding: Inward pulling of the suprasternal notch

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue and nail beds in good light
findings.finding: Bluish discoloration of the lips and mucous membranes

findings.maneuver: Auscultate both lung fields with a small-bore stethoscope
findings.finding: Breath sounds are diminished bilaterally, especially at the bases

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lung bases during inspiration
findings.finding: Fine inspiratory crackles at the bases

findings.maneuver: Palpate the precordium and auscultate heart sounds
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 with no gallop or thrill

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant and liver edge
findings.finding: Liver edge not enlarged for age

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, nails and umbilical cord for meconium staining
findings.finding: No meconium staining of skin or nails

findings.maneuver: Measure axillary temperature and assess for temperature instability
Observe the infant's level of alertness and response to handling
findings.finding: Reduced spontaneous activity and poor feeding

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin color and perfusion
findings.finding: Cool, mottled skin with prolonged capillary refill

findings.maneuver: Observe breathing continuously on the monitor
findings.finding: Pauses in breathing lasting more than 20 seconds

findings.maneuver: Observe the head and neck during breathing

labs.caveat: Respiratory acidosis from alveolar collapse and CO2 retention; a normal pH does not exclude the diagnosis early on.
Rising PaCO2 signals fatigue and impending respiratory failure.
Hypoxemia that improves with supplemental oxygen but often requires positive pressure; a large alveolar-arterial gradient is typical.
Metabolic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion or lactic acid; a negative base excess suggests a mixed picture.
Elevated with hypoperfusion or sepsis; helps distinguish from transient tachypnea.
Hypoglycemia is common in premature and growth-restricted infants and can worsen respiratory distress; treat promptly.
Leukopenia or neutropenia may reflect sepsis rather than RDS itself; a normal or elevated count does not exclude infection.
Thrombocytopenia may accompany sepsis, asphyxia or disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Nonspecific; a rise over 24–48 hours supports infection but does not rule out RDS.

findings.text: Diffuse, fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) opacities throughout both lungs
Air bronchograms extending beyond the perihilar region
Low lung volumes with a small, bell-shaped thorax
Whiteout of both lungs (complete opacification) in severe disease
Pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum (air leak from positive pressure ventilation)

imaging.preferred_when: Bedside assessment when transfer for x-ray is undesirable

findings.text: Bilateral confluent B-lines with a white lung appearance
Thickened pleura with a double lung point
Normal cardiac anatomy with no structural defect
Right-to-left or bidirectional shunt across a patent ductus arteriosus or foramen ovale
Elevated pulmonary artery pressure suggesting persistent pulmonary hypertension

initial.why: Confirms hypoxemia and respiratory acidosis and guides oxygen and ventilation support
Detects hypoglycemia, which is common in premature infants and worsens distress
Baseline blood count and looks for leukopenia or thrombocytopenia suggesting sepsis
Shows the classic ground-glass pattern and air bronchograms and excludes other causes of distress
Assesses electrolytes, calcium and renal function in a premature infant

supporting.why: Supports or argues against concurrent infection when sepsis is a concern
Assesses perfusion and helps distinguish from transient tachypnea
Evaluates for congenital heart disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension
supporting.only_if: cyanosis is disproportionate to the lung findings, a murmur is heard, or hypoxemia persists despite adequate ventilation

supporting.why: Bedside alternative when x-ray is not immediately available
supporting.only_if: the infant is too unstable to leave the unit for imaging

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for suspected cardiac disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension
not_indicated.only_if: cyanosis is disproportionate to the lung findings, a murmur is heard, or hypoxemia persists despite adequate ventilation

not_indicated.why: Not routine when chest x-ray is available
not_indicated.only_if: the infant is too unstable to leave the unit for imaging

not_indicated.why: Lumbar puncture is not part of the RDS workup; reserved for suspected meningitis
No role in neonatal respiratory distress
Not indicated in the initial evaluation of RDS
Not part of the acute respiratory distress workup

decision_points: Blood gas and chest x-ray are the key initial tests; the diagnosis is clinical and radiographic
If the infant is unstable or has apnea, support ventilation before completing the workup
Consider sepsis and start antibiotics if there are risk factors for infection, since it can mimic RDS
Echocardiography is reserved for suspected congenital heart disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: Presents with respiratory distress, tachypnea, grunting, temperature instability and lethargy in a newborn, and can coexist with or mimic RDS.
differential.trigger: Fever or temperature instability, maternal chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes, or an infant who is more ill than the lung findings suggest

history: Onset may be later than the first few hours
exam: Lethargy and poor perfusion out of proportion to lung findings
labs: Elevated CRP that rises over 24-48 hours
imaging: Chest x-ray may be normal or show patchy infiltrates rather than diffuse ground-glass

differential.name: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
differential.why_considered: Most common cause of early respiratory distress in near-term and term infants, with tachypnea and mild retractions shortly after birth.

history: Symptoms begin within hours of birth and resolve within 24-72 hours
exam: Tachypnea with minimal grunting or retractions
Usually pink on room air or low-flow oxygen
imaging: Perihilar streaking and fluid in the interlobar fissures

differential.name: Meconium aspiration syndrome
differential.why_considered: Respiratory distress in a newborn with tachypnea, grunting and hypoxemia, often in term or post-term infants.

exam: Meconium staining of skin, nails and umbilical cord
imaging: Patchy, coarse infiltrates with areas of hyperinflation
Air leak (pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum) may be present

differential.name: Congenital pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Respiratory distress with tachypnea, grunting and hypoxemia in a newborn, often with risk factors for infection.

history: May present at or shortly after birth
labs: Positive blood culture or tracheal aspirate culture

differential.name: Congenital heart disease (cyanotic)
differential.why_considered: Cyanosis and respiratory distress in a newborn that can mimic RDS, especially with hypoxemia.
differential.trigger: Cyanosis disproportionate to lung findings, a heart murmur, or hypoxemia that does not improve with supplemental oxygen

history: Prenatal diagnosis or family history of congenital heart disease
No or minimal respiratory distress despite marked cyanosis
exam: Difference in blood pressure or oxygen saturation between arms and legs
labs: Hypoxemia that does not improve with supplemental oxygen
imaging: Chest x-ray may show abnormal cardiac silhouette or pulmonary vascularity

differential.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
differential.why_considered: Severe hypoxemia and cyanosis in a newborn, often with respiratory distress, that can mimic or complicate RDS.

exam: Normal or mildly abnormal lung exam
labs: Severe hypoxemia with a large alveolar-arterial gradient
Pre- and postductal oxygen saturation difference
imaging: Echocardiogram shows elevated pulmonary artery pressure and right-to-left or bidirectional shunt

severity.mild: Tachypnea and mild retractions with oxygen requirement less than 30% and no apnea; resolves over 2-3 days
severity.moderate: Marked grunting, retractions and cyanosis requiring supplemental oxygen and nasal CPAP; respiratory acidosis on blood gas
severity.severe: Severe distress with apnea, requiring mechanical ventilation and surfactant; chest x-ray shows diffuse ground-glass opacities or whiteout
severity.critical: Respiratory failure with refractory hypoxemia, shock, or air leak syndrome; may require high-frequency ventilation or ECMO

red_flags.meaning: Impending respiratory failure; needs immediate ventilation
Respiratory muscle fatigue; consider mechanical ventilation
Suggests persistent pulmonary hypertension or congenital heart disease

red_flags.finding: Sudden deterioration with asymmetric breath sounds

red_flags.meaning: Sepsis or shock; start antibiotics and volume resuscitation

complications.name: Pneumothorax
clues: Transillumination or x-ray showing air outside the lung

complications.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
clues: Ongoing oxygen requirement beyond 28 days of life
Chronic lung disease on chest x-ray

complications.name: Retinopathy of prematurity
clues: Abnormal retinal vascularization on screening exam

special_populations.differences: Late preterm and near-term infants may have milder or delayed symptoms, sometimes presenting after 6 hours of age with only tachypnea and mild retractions.
Infants of diabetic mothers may develop respiratory distress despite being near term or term, and may have macrosomia and hypoglycemia.

key_questions.question: How many weeks pregnant were you when you delivered, and what was the baby's birth weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity, especially before 28-30 weeks; lower gestational age and birth weight mean higher risk

key_questions.question: When did the breathing trouble start after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Within minutes to the first few hours; present by 6 hours of age in nearly all affected infants

key_questions.question: What does the breathing look like - is there grunting, flaring, or pulling in of the chest?
key_questions.looking_for: Grunting, nasal flaring and retractions that worsen over the first day

key_questions.question: Has the breathing gotten worse, stayed the same, or improved since it started?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive worsening over the first 24-72 hours, then gradual improvement with treatment

key_questions.question: Was the delivery vaginal or cesarean, and was there labor before the cesarean?
key_questions.looking_for: Cesarean delivery without preceding labor increases risk

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, including gestational diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: Infant of a diabetic mother is at higher risk even near term

key_questions.question: Was the amniotic fluid meconium-stained, foul-smelling, or was there prolonged rupture of membranes?
key_questions.looking_for: Meconium aspiration or chorioamnionitis as alternative or coexisting causes

key_questions.question: Did you have any fever, infection, or chorioamnionitis around the time of delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal infection raising concern for neonatal sepsis or congenital pneumonia

key_questions.question: Did the baby need any resuscitation, suctioning, or oxygen in the delivery room?
key_questions.looking_for: Perinatal asphyxia or need for positive pressure ventilation

key_questions.question: Is the baby feeding, and how is his energy level?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding and lethargy, which may be from distress or suggest sepsis

key_questions.question: Has the baby had a fever, low temperature, or been unusually floppy?
key_questions.looking_for: Temperature instability or lethargy suggesting sepsis rather than RDS alone

key_questions.question: Did a previous baby have breathing problems or respiratory distress syndrome after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of RDS in a sibling

accepted_names: Respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn
reasoning_points: Premature infant with onset of tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring and retractions within the first few hours of life
Progressive worsening over the first 24-72 hours consistent with surfactant deficiency and alveolar collapse
Risk factors such as prematurity, low birth weight, infant of a diabetic mother, or cesarean delivery without labor
Hypoxemia with respiratory acidosis on blood gas and an elevated alveolar-arterial gradient
Chest x-ray showing diffuse fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) opacities, air bronchograms and low lung volumes
No fever, no meconium staining, no murmur and no hepatomegaly, arguing against sepsis, meconium aspiration and congenital heart disease
Improvement with supplemental oxygen, positive pressure support and surfactant therapy

easy: Very premature infant (before 30 weeks) with immediate grunting, retractions and nasal flaring after delivery
Classic chest x-ray with diffuse ground-glass opacities and air bronchograms
Clear prematurity risk factors and no signs of infection
medium: Late preterm infant with milder or delayed symptoms appearing after 6 hours of age
Infant of a diabetic mother who is near term but develops distress
Concurrent concern for sepsis requiring antibiotics while RDS is also treated
Chest x-ray with findings that overlap with transient tachypnea of the newborn
hard: Term infant with respiratory distress where congenital heart disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension must be excluded
Infant with meconium-stained fluid and patchy infiltrates rather than classic ground-glass
Sudden deterioration from pneumothorax or air leak complicating the picture
Infant with hypoxemia refractory to oxygen suggesting persistent pulmonary hypertension or a cardiac lesion
